Google has come under fire after confirming that its Android systems could infer a user’s location from nearby mobile mast data, even when location services were switched off and the SIM card had been removed. The finding raised fresh concerns among privacy advocates, who argued that many users would reasonably expect their phones to stop sharing such information once tracking settings were disabled.

According to the report, Android devices had been collecting Cell ID data along with country and network codes as part of a background messaging function tied to Google’s Firebase Cloud Messaging service. Google said the information was being tested to improve message delivery and battery efficiency, but it later stated that the data was immediately discarded and that the feature had been changed so it would no longer request Cell ID.

Still, the episode highlighted how much can be learned from routine network signals. By combining mast locations with other network details, a rough position could be estimated, and in some urban areas the result could be much more precise. For many users, that created a troubling gap between the privacy they thought they had and the data their phones were still sending.

Consumer groups called for clearer disclosure and stronger controls, saying companies should make it obvious when a background service can infer location. They also urged regulators to examine whether users had been given enough choice. Google’s return response emphasized that the issue had been addressed, but the controversy showed how quickly trust can fade when a hidden body of data collection comes to light.

In the end, the story became less about a technical feature and more about consent, transparency, and the limits of privacy on modern devices.
